notes.front: What is USCIS, in one sentence?
notes.back: United States Citizenship and Immigration Services: the Department of Homeland Security agency that gives the naturalization civics test.
notes.explanation: USCIS gives the test, so its officer asks the questions and checks your answers.
notes.example: Like the DMV runs driving tests, USCIS runs the citizenship test.

notes.front: What is naturalization?
notes.back: The legal process by which a person becomes a US citizen after birth, rather than by being born a citizen.
notes.explanation: It is the process the civics test is part of: passing the test is one requirement for naturalizing.
notes.example: Example: Maria was born in Mexico, got a Green Card, and later became a US citizen. That is naturalization.

notes.front: What is a lawful permanent resident (LPR)?
notes.back: A person lawfully allowed to live in the United States permanently as an immigrant.
notes.explanation: Most people must be LPRs before they can apply, so LPR status normally comes before the civics test.
notes.example: Like a Green Card holder who has lived and worked in the US for years but has not yet applied for citizenship.

notes.front: What is Form N-400?
notes.back: The application form for naturalization; its filing date decides which version of the civics test an applicant takes.
notes.explanation: The 20 October 2025 filing-date cutoff (below) is measured against this form's filing date.
notes.source: Policy Manual, Vol. 12 Part E Ch. 2
notes.example: Like filing a job application on a certain date, which decides which year's hiring rules apply to you.

notes.front: What does "civics" mean on the naturalization test?
notes.back: Knowledge and understanding of the fundamentals of US history and of the principles and form of government of the United States.
notes.explanation: These are the words of the law that the civics test checks.
notes.example: Like a driving test checks road knowledge, the civics test checks knowledge of US history and government.

notes.front: What is the 2025 Naturalization Civics Test?
notes.back: The current oral civics test: up to 20 questions from a bank of 128, needing 12 correct to pass.
notes.explanation: It uses the same 128 questions as the 2020 test. Only one thing changed: when the officer stops.
notes.example: Like a driving test drawing 20 questions at random from a published question bank of 128.

notes.front: What is the 2008 Naturalization Civics Test?
notes.back: The previous civics test: 100 questions, 10 asked, 6 to pass; still given to applicants who filed before 20 October 2025.
notes.explanation: Two versions are live at once: which one an applicant takes depends only on when they filed Form N-400.
notes.source: Policy Manual, Vol. 12 Part E Ch. 2; 90 FR 45050
notes.example: Like an older exam syllabus that some students are still tested on because they enrolled before the new syllabus began.

notes.front: What is the "oral test" format of the civics test?
notes.back: The USCIS officer asks each question aloud and the applicant answers aloud, during the naturalization interview.
notes.explanation: For the civics part, you do not write. You only speak.
notes.example: Like a spoken language exam, rather than a multiple-choice sheet.

notes.front: What is the civics test's stopping rule?
notes.back: The officer stops the test once the applicant has answered 12 questions correctly (a pass) or 9 incorrectly (a fail).
notes.explanation: This is the one change 2025 made to how the 2020 test was given: the 2020 test asked all 20 questions regardless.
notes.example: Example: you get 12 right after 14 questions. The officer stops. You passed.

notes.front: What is 65/20 special consideration?
notes.back: Age 65 or older, resident 20 or more years: study 20 questions, answer 10, need 6 right, any language.
notes.explanation: It lowers the study load and the passing count, and removes the English requirement for the test itself.
notes.example: Like an older, long-time applicant being tested on a shorter, marked-out study list.

notes.front: What is an interpreter's role on the civics test?
notes.back: A person who translates the questions and answers when an applicant is allowed to take the test in another language.
notes.explanation: 65/20 applicants, and some others exempt from English, may use one; most applicants may not.
notes.example: Like a translator sitting in on an oral exam given in the applicant's own language.

notes.front: What is the English exemption (50/20 and 55/15)?
notes.back: Applicants over 50 with 20 years, or over 55 with 15 years, as an LPR skip the English test but must still pass civics.
notes.explanation: It shows the English and civics requirements are separate: this exemption never excuses civics.
notes.example: Example: Ahmed is 56 and has had a Green Card for 16 years. He does not take the English test, but he must still take the civics test.

notes.front: What happens if an applicant fails the civics test the first time?
notes.back: USCIS gives a second opportunity, or re-examination, within 90 days of the first examination.
notes.explanation: The Policy Manual narrows this: the second test comes between 60 and 90 days after the first.
notes.source: 8 CFR 312.5(a); Policy Manual Vol. 12 Part E Ch. 2
notes.example: Example: you fail in March. Your second test is in May or June.

notes.front: What is the disability exception (Form N-648)?
notes.back: If a doctor certifies that a disability stops you from learning civics, Form N-648 can excuse you from the civics test.
notes.explanation: It is a separate route around the requirement, not a version of the test itself.
notes.example: Like a medical exemption form that removes a requirement entirely, rather than making it easier.

notes.front: What are USCIS "test updates"?
notes.back: A USCIS page listing current answers to questions that change with elections or appointments; answer with the official serving at interview time.
notes.explanation: Officials' names are not fixed facts: they must be checked close to the interview, not memorised once.
notes.source: M-1778 p.1; Check for Test Updates
notes.example: Like checking today's weather instead of trusting yesterday's forecast.

notes.front: How many questions are in the 2025 civics test bank?
notes.explanation: A 2025 USCIS policy alert raised the bank from 100 (2008 test) to 128 for the 2025 test.

notes.front: How many questions can the officer ask on the 2025 test?
notes.back: Up to 20.
notes.explanation: The 20 are drawn at random from the 128-question bank.

notes.front: How many correct answers are needed to pass the 2025 test?
notes.back: 12 (out of 20).
notes.explanation: 12 of 20 is the 60% pass mark, unchanged from earlier versions.

notes.front: How many wrong answers make the officer stop the 2025 test as a fail?
notes.explanation: With 9 wrong, you can get at most 11 right out of 20, so you cannot reach 12.

notes.front: What pass percentage does the civics test use?
notes.explanation: 60% has stayed the same across the 2008, 2020 and 2025 versions, even though the totals changed.

notes.front: From which N-400 filing date does the 2025 test apply?
notes.back: 20 October 2025.
notes.explanation: Applicants who filed before that date take the 2008 test instead.

notes.front: How long after the 18 September 2025 notice did USCIS wait before applying the 2025 test?
notes.back: 30 days.
notes.explanation: This gave applicants who filed soon after the notice time to prepare for whichever test applied to them.

notes.front: What age and years as an LPR qualify an applicant for 65/20 special consideration?
notes.back: Age 65 or older, and 20 or more years as a lawful permanent resident, both at filing.
notes.explanation: Both conditions are measured at the date Form N-400 is filed, not at the interview.

notes.front: How many questions does a 65/20 applicant study, get asked, and need correct?
notes.back: 20 studied (asterisked), 10 asked, 6 correct.
notes.explanation: The pass rate is the same as the standard test: 60%.

notes.front: The 2008 test: how many questions are in the list, how many are asked, how many must be right, and when does the officer stop?
notes.back: 100 in the bank, 10 asked, 6 correct to pass, stopping at 5 wrong.
notes.explanation: The 2008 test's proportions (10 asked, 6 to pass) are the same shape as the 2025 test's, only smaller.

notes.front: Within how many days of the first test must a failed applicant get a second try?
notes.back: 90 days.
notes.explanation: This is the outer limit; the Policy Manual narrows the window further (next card).

notes.front: What is the narrower window USCIS gives for a second civics test?
notes.back: Between 60 and 90 days after the first examination.
notes.explanation: USCIS shall not require the applicant to appear for a re-examination earlier than 60 days after the first examination.
notes.source: Policy Manual, Vol. 12 Part E Ch. 2; 8 CFR 335.3(b)

notes.front: An applicant wants to know which federal agency will interview them and score their civics answers. Who is it?
notes.back: USCIS (US Citizenship and Immigration Services), part of the Department of Homeland Security.
notes.explanation: USCIS both writes the questions and administers the interview, so it controls every rule in this topic.

notes.front: A Green Card holder wants to become a US citizen. What is that legal process called?
notes.back: Naturalization.
notes.explanation: It names the process the civics test sits inside, distinct from simply keeping LPR status.

notes.front: Before applying to naturalize, what status must most applicants already hold?
notes.back: Lawful permanent resident (LPR).
notes.explanation: Naturalization is a change of status from LPR to citizen, so LPR status normally comes first.

notes.front: Two applicants have identical LPR histories. One files Form N-400 on 1 October 2025, the other on 25 October 2025. Which civics test does each take?
notes.back: The 1 October filer takes the 2008 test; the 25 October filer takes the 2025 test.
notes.explanation: Only the Form N-400 filing date, against the 20 October 2025 cutoff, decides the version.
notes.choices:
A) Both take the 2025 test
B) Both take the 2008 test
C) The 1 October filer takes 2008, the 25 October filer takes 2025
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the 1 October filing is before the 20 October 2025 cutoff. B is wrong because the 25 October filing is on or after the cutoff.

notes.front: The civics test checks understanding of which two subjects?
notes.back: US history, and the principles and form of US government.
notes.explanation: These are the words of the law that the civics test checks.

notes.front: An applicant is told they will be asked up to 20 questions from a bank of 128 and need 12 right. Which test are they taking?
notes.back: The 2025 Naturalization Civics Test.
notes.explanation: The 128-question bank and the 20/12 numbers only belong to the 2025 version.

notes.front: An applicant filed Form N-400 in September 2025. Which civics test do they take?
notes.back: The 2008 Naturalization Civics Test.
notes.explanation: Their filing was before the 20 October 2025 cutoff, so the older, 100-question test still applies to them.

notes.front: Can an applicant write their civics answers on paper instead of speaking them?
notes.back: No. The officer asks and the applicant answers aloud.
notes.explanation: The test is oral by regulation, given in English except for stated exceptions.

notes.front: An applicant on the 2025 test has answered 12 questions correctly after only 15 questions. What does the officer do?
notes.back: Stop the test: the applicant has already passed.
notes.explanation: The 2025 stopping rule ends the test as soon as 12 correct (pass) or 9 wrong (fail) is reached.
notes.choices:
A) Stop, the applicant has passed
B) Ask all 20 questions anyway
C) Ask 5 more to be sure
notes.choicesExplained: B describes the 2020 test's rule, not the 2025 rule. C is not a documented USCIS practice.

notes.front: An applicant is 68 and has held a Green Card for 22 years, both true when she filed Form N-400. What does 65/20 consideration give her?
notes.back: A 20-question study list, 10 questions asked, 6 needed to pass, and testing in any language she chooses.
notes.explanation: 65/20 special consideration eases the format and language of the test; it does not remove the requirement.
notes.choices:
A) A shorter study list and language choice
B) An automatic pass
C) Exemption from the civics test entirely
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: she must still answer correctly. C is wrong: only Form N-648 exempts civics entirely, and that requires a qualifying impairment, not age.

notes.front: An applicant fails the civics test at the first interview. What happens next?
notes.back: USCIS schedules a second test, between 60 and 90 days after the first.
notes.explanation: The applicant is not automatically denied: the regulations guarantee one more attempt.
notes.source: 8 CFR 312.5(a); Policy Manual Vol. 12 Part E Ch. 2

notes.front: An applicant memorised the Speaker of the House's name from a study guide printed two years ago. Is that answer safe to give at interview?
notes.back: Not necessarily: they must give the name of the official actually serving at the time of the interview, checked against USCIS test updates.
notes.explanation: USCIS tells applicants to verify volatile answers against its test-updates page shortly before the interview.
notes.source: M-1778 p.1; Check for Test Updates
notes.choices:
A) Check uscis.gov/citizenship/testupdates before the interview
B) Trust the study guide, it is official
C) Give either name, both count
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because officials change with elections and appointments after a guide is printed. C is wrong: only the official serving at interview time is correct.

notes.front: What is the difference between the 2008 and 2025 Naturalization Civics Tests?
notes.back: 2008: 100-question bank, 10 asked, 6 to pass, stop at 5 wrong. 2025: 128-question bank, 20 asked, 12 to pass, stop at 9 wrong.
notes.explanation: The pass rate (60%) and the spoken format are the same. The numbers and the questions are different.
notes.contrast: Which test an applicant takes depends solely on their Form N-400 filing date, not on when they interview.

notes.front: What is the difference between the standard 2025 test and the 65/20 version?
notes.back: Standard: 20 of 128 asked, 12 to pass, usually in English. 65/20: 10 of 20 marked questions asked, 6 to pass, any language.
notes.explanation: The 65/20 format applies under either the 2008 or 2025 question bank, whichever the applicant's filing date sets.
notes.contrast: 65/20 eligibility depends on age and years as an LPR at filing, not on which test version applies.
